_what_this_is: The entry gate, answered BEFORE drafting. The threshold question is whether a well-informed non-expert would confidently believe something the primary sources do not support.

belief._note: What the reader already believes, stated as they would state it. If you cannot write this sentence, there is nothing to correct and no subject -- which is how the tobacco-analogy candidate died.
belief.statement: Inclusive education is the right approach. Programmes that train teachers, make schools physically accessible, and provide assistive devices like glasses, hearing aids or wheelchairs get more disabled children into school and learning. Putting children in mainstream classrooms with support works better than separate special schools.
belief.how_we_know_they_believe_it: The coverage that settled it. Named outlets, quoted headlines. Not 'it is widely assumed'.

what_the_sources_show._note: What the primary sources actually support, and which sources.

direction._note: CORRECTS, CONFIRMS or NARROWS. This field exists so the contrarianism guard can count. A publication whose answer is always CORRECTS is performing scepticism rather than assessing evidence, and is not to be trusted.

reader_with_a_decision: Education ministry planners, donor and NGO programme officers, and disability organisations in low- and middle-income countries. They are deciding which disability-inclusive education interventions to fund, scale or design, and whether to invest in mainstream inclusion, specialised provision, assistive technology or teacher training.

public_record_check._note: NOT 'has anybody published this'. On any contested question, somebody has. The question is whether it has been carried WHERE THIS READER WOULD FIND IT. Run the counterexample hunter on the belief statement, not on the finding.
public_record_check.our_contribution: translation, extension, or correction of the prior art -- say which

kill_condition: Rigorous evaluations from low- and middle-income countries (randomised or well-controlled studies, and systematic reviews of them) consistently find that these programmes improve enrolment, attendance and learning for children with disabilities. They also clearly identify the same programme types the belief favours (teacher training, accessibility, assistive devices, mainstream inclusion) as most effective, with moderate or high certainty. If so, the common belief is simply confirmed and there is no story.

kill_condition_tested._note: Filled in AFTER going to look, by whoever looked.

scope._note: What the answer will and will not cover, written at step 1 BEFORE any source is opened, so scope cannot be fitted to the findings afterwards. An omission ruled OUT_OF_SCOPE, and a headline conclusion declared out of scope, must name the question's words or one of these entries (fix 2, docs/whu-fix2-omission-rulings-design.md section 2.4).
scope.covers: Whether interventions designed to improve educational access, participation or learning outcomes for children and young people with disabilities in low- and middle-income countries achieve those outcomes, and how effectiveness compares across intervention types. Intervention types include teacher training, inclusive-education models, special schools, assistive devices, community-based rehabilitation, cash transfers, parent and community programmes, and early childhood interventions.

out.what: Whether inclusive education is a human right or a legal obligation under the CRPD
out.why: That is a normative and legal question, not an empirical question about what works.

out.what: Effectiveness of disability-inclusive education programmes in high-income countries
out.why: The question is limited to low- and middle-income settings, where context, resources and systems differ substantially.

out.what: Prevalence of disability and the size of the education gap for disabled children
out.why: This describes the problem rather than evaluating interventions. It may be used only as background.

out.what: Health or rehabilitation outcomes of interventions (e.g. functional improvement from therapy) not linked to education

out.why: This is a separate economic question. Cost data may be noted but will not be systematically weighed.

evidence_standard._note: What kinds of evidence the answer will weigh, written at step 1 BEFORE any source is opened (post-study fix 3, docs/whu-fix3-evidence-standard.md). 'measured': outcomes measured in trials, cohorts, evaluations. 'assessed': expert assessments -- systematic-review conclusions, IPCC confidence-rated statements, guideline recommendations. When they differ, the page states both and drops neither.
evidence_standard.measured: Quantitative effects on enrolment, attendance, retention, completion and learning outcomes (test scores, literacy, numeracy) for children and young people with disabilities. These come from randomised trials, quasi-experimental evaluations and controlled before-after studies in low- and middle-income countries, including effect sizes, sample sizes and comparison conditions.
evidence_standard.assessed: Certainty or confidence ratings that systematic reviews, evidence and gap maps, or expert panels assign to the body of evidence on each intervention type (e.g. GRADE ratings, risk-of-bias judgements, statements that evidence is insufficient). Also included are reviewers' judgements about which intervention categories have adequate evidence and which remain gaps.
